blocks.text: Quick verdict

These two are close, and the right pick depends on your workload. Oxylabs has the larger advertised residential pool (175M+ against 150M+), a published 99.95% success rate, cheaper entry through its $30 Starter plan, and a $2.50/GB Corporate rate. Bright Data offers deeper targeting (carrier as well as ZIP and ASN), a broader managed product line including the Scraping Browser and datasets, and frequent half-price PAYG promotions. Pick Oxylabs for raw scale and simpler entry; pick Bright Data for the widest toolset.

Bright Data and Oxylabs are the two names every enterprise data team shortlists. Both sell residential, datacenter, ISP and mobile networks, both run pools well above 100 million IPs, and both offer managed scraping products that bill per result rather than per gigabyte. The differences are in pricing structure, targeting depth, product breadth and how each handles onboarding. This comparison breaks those differences down so you can choose the right enterprise partner.

blocks.text: Bright Data in 2026: what you get

Bright Data, formerly Luminati, is the default enterprise pick for teams that want every collection tool under one contract. Its residential pool is one of the deepest available (150M+ advertised IPs across 195 countries), targeting goes down to city, ZIP and ASN, and the company layers managed products such as Web Unlocker and the Scraping Browser on top. You pay for that breadth: entry pricing is the highest of the major providers unless a promotion is running, and access to some target categories requires a compliance review.

Strengths: Deepest targeting in the market (ZIP, ASN, carrier); Managed unblocking, SERP and browser products under one account; Mature compliance and KYC processes that enterprise buyers ask for; Very large residential pool for high-rotation work. Weak spots: Highest list price per GB at low volume; Dashboard and zone setup take time to learn; Some targets need a compliance review before access.
Oxylabs in 2026: what you get

Oxylabs is a Lithuanian web-data company and Bright Data's closest rival at the top of the market. It advertises a residential pool of more than 175 million IPs across 195 locations, publishes a 99.95% success rate for residential traffic, and sells seven product lines including datacenter, ISP and mobile proxies, a Web Scraper API and Web Unblocker. Onboarding is more sales-led than the mid-market providers, but self-service has expanded through 2026, including dedicated ISP proxies.

Strengths: One of the two largest residential pools available; Published 99.95% residential success rate; Strong scraper APIs that bill per result; Formal ethical-sourcing documentation for procurement. Weak spots: Expensive at low volume ($8/GB PAYG); Best rates need large monthly commitments; Residential trial goes through sales rather than self-service.
Pricing: Bright Data vs Oxylabs

Bright Data lists residential traffic at $8/GB pay-as-you-go with no commitment, and it frequently runs 50%-off promotions that bring that to about $4/GB. Monthly plans start with the Growth tier at $499 for roughly 141 GB (about $3.50/GB) and fall to around $2.50/GB on the largest public plan.

Oxylabs charges $8/GB pay-as-you-go for residential traffic. Monthly plans start with Starter at $30 for 5 GB ($6/GB) and a Basic tier around $100 for 20 GB, and the rate falls to $2.50/GB on the $2,500/month Corporate plan. Mobile traffic starts at $7.50/GB.

For 10 GB, there is little to separate them on price ($80 for Bright Data, $80 for Oxylabs). At 100 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because Oxylabs does not publish an exact price for that volume; Bright Data comes to about $499. Both Bright Data and Oxylabs work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

On paper the two networks are similar in size: Bright Data advertises 150M+ residential IPs and Oxylabs advertises 175M+. Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, Bright Data lists 195 countries and Oxylabs lists 195. On targeting, Bright Data offers country, state, city, ZIP, ASN and carrier, while Oxylabs offers country, state, city, ZIP and ASN.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, Bright Data offers rotating per request or sticky sessions you control per zone, and Oxylabs offers rotating and sticky sessions on residential and mobile. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. Bright Data: its pool depth and Web Unlocker handle hardened targets. Oxylabs: its pool size and Web Scraper API suit large crawls. Let price and the countries you need decide.

SERP and rank tracking: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Bright Data: it sells a dedicated SERP API alongside raw proxies. With Oxylabs: its scraper API returns parsed search results. Run the same small test on both before committing.

Social media and multi-account management: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Bright Data: it is powerful but expensive for low-volume account work. With Oxylabs: it works, but the pricing is built for volume, not a handful of accounts. Run the same small test on both before committing.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Bright Data: ZIP-level targeting suits local pricing and stock checks. With Oxylabs: city and ZIP targeting plus parsed e-commerce endpoints. Run the same small test on both before committing.
Ad verification and geo-testing: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: carrier and ASN targeting reproduce what real users see. How Oxylabs compares: broad geo coverage with ASN targeting.

Tight budgets: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Bright Data: its list price is the highest in this comparison. With Oxylabs: entry pricing is among the highest in this comparison. Run the same small test on both before committing.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Bright Data: Free trial for business accounts, no card required. Oxylabs: Residential trial arranged through sales, once per customer. Verification and payment rules differ too. Bright Data: Verification required for some sensitive targets. Oxylabs: Business verification on larger accounts. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Bright Data and Oxylabs before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle Bright Data vs Oxylabs faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Bright Data: free trial for business accounts, no card required; Oxylabs: residential trial arranged through sales, once per customer).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.

3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country. 4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Bright Data comes out ahead in 1, Oxylabs in 0, and 5 are ties. That makes Bright Data the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Bright Data is strongest for enterprise data teams with budget for managed tooling, while Oxylabs is strongest for large scraping pipelines with steady volume. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
